stories.story_title: AI assistance enters the Bering Sea pollock assessment review record
stories.summary_2_sentences: A NOAA Alaska Fisheries Science Center working paper dated September 3rd recommends Model 26.0 for the November and December assessment review. It explicitly discloses AI assistance in document development and model implementation, with authors retaining scientific responsibility.
stories.why_it_matters_to_alaskans: The eastern Bering Sea pollock assessment informs catch-limit advice; reproducible model changes have direct fishery relevance.

sources.author: James Ianelli; Sophia Wassermann; Carey McGilliard; Grant Adams; Matt Cheng; Cody Szuwalski; Cole Monnahan
sources.fetch_method: Python urllib HTTPS; web search discovered source, direct web open errored

exact_facts: Comparison data cover 1964 to 2024; new 2025 and 2026 observations await quality checks.
47 of 50 dispersed-start fits reached the best solution; all 50 simulated-data self-tests converged.
Separate FT-NIRS age-data comparisons flag lower cohort consistency than traditional microscope ages; consequence remains unresolved.
stories.quote: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools were used to aid document development and model implementation.
visual_story_fuel: Bering Sea pollock silhouette to otolith rings to scientific review table.
Fifty fit markers: 47 at best solution, three at alternative objective.
Model-comparison plots are embedded in the working paper.
caveats: Recommendation, not adoption or a new catch limit.
AI is documented as authoring/code assistance; Rceattle itself is not established here as an AI predictor.
FT-NIRS is a separate measurement-method issue, not proof of a newly deployed AI system.
stories.dedupe_status: Not among supplied excluded subjects; confirm run ledger.
stories.editorial_strength: moderate: strongest clean science lead, but AI role is assisted scientific work rather than autonomous decision-making

stories.story_title: NOAA sets a calibration-first path for autonomous fisheries surveys
stories.summary_2_sentences: A September 3rd NOAA feature presents an Alaska Fisheries Science Center-led framework for integrating autonomous vehicles, optics, acoustics, and eDNA with conventional surveys. Parallel tests preserve comparability with historical stock-assessment data.
stories.why_it_matters_to_alaskans: Alaska pollock surveys and North Pacific rockfish sampling are concrete examples; new platforms could expand coverage.

sources.author: NOAA Fisheries; Stan Kotwicki quoted as framework lead author

exact_facts: NOAA documents an earlier acoustic-only Saildrone pollock survey when COVID curtailed conventional surveys.
The article says AFSC is exploring uncrewed vehicles working alongside research vessels.
stories.quote: And one of the biggest challenges is maintaining data consistency and continuity.
visual_story_fuel: DriX H-8 alongside NOAA Ship Oscar Dyson.
Dutch Harbor Saildrone and stereo-camera frame.
Paired conventional and autonomous survey paths.
caveats: Framework report, not a new Alaska deployment announcement.
CROSS-SURFACE REPEAT: Alaska AI carousel published this same framework on September 6th. Do not treat it as a clean fresh lead without editorial clearance.
